items.title: Ex-officer's double murder trial tests self-defence law (ABC, 3 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Jamie McKinnell, ABC News, 3 November 2026, reporting R v Lamarre-Condon (NSW Supreme Court, Adams J, jury trial); Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) ss 18, 418–421
items.significance: A former police officer accused of two murders with his service pistol runs self-defence: the Crown must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt, and excessive self-defence could reduce murder to manslaughter.
core_labels: The role of juries, including verdicts
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - Lamarre-Condon Double Murder Trial Self-Defence Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Former NSW police officer **Beau Lamarre-Condon** has pleaded not guilty to the **murders** of Jesse Baird and Luke
Davies, allegedly shot with his police pistol on 19 February 2024; he surrendered at Bondi four days later and has
been in custody since. The jury trial is expected to run about three months. On 3 November a police officer's
statement of what the accused told police was read to the jury. **He is presumed innocent; nothing has been
decided.**
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.3.8 (defences)** — self-defence and excessive self-defence in a live jury trial; pair with *Zecevic*.
- **crime.3.6** — the burden of disproof on the Crown.
- **crime.3.9** — a jury deciding contested facts; reports differ on whether 12 or 15 jurors are sitting.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of one day of Crown evidence**; the defence case had not been heard. Treat the victims'
families with care. Check the verdict before using any outcome.

sections.Crown v defence (as opened):
| | Crown | Defence |
|---|---|---|
| Why he entered | Planned to kill Mr Baird after an alleged obsession | Went to collect belongings |
| The pistol | Taken from a Balmain station locker on 16 February | Carried because protocol barred leaving it in a car |
| Shootings | Three shots; Mr Davies killed to leave no witness | Two struggles over the gun, Mr Baird first with a knife |
| Afterwards | Deliberate cover-up | Panic after the deaths |
| Result sought | Murder, self-defence excluded beyond reasonable doubt | Not guilty — self-defence |
sections.The law:
Self-defence (s 418) is a complete defence if the accused believed the conduct necessary and it was a reasonable
response to the circumstances as perceived. Once raised, the **Crown must disprove it** beyond reasonable doubt
(s 419). If the belief was genuine but the response unreasonable, **excessive self-defence** (s 421) reduces murder to
manslaughter. Agreed facts include the disguise and moving the bodies.

items.title: Human Rights Watch finds SA prisons isolate prisoners with disabilities (1 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Human Rights Watch, 'They Just Locked Me Away: Solitary Confinement and Abuse of People with Disabilities in Prisons in the State of South Australia' (report and news release, 1 November 2026); Correctional Services Act 1982 (SA) ss 20–20G, 36; Mandela Rules 43–45; Convention against Torture; CRPD arts 9, 14
items.significance: Twelve of 14 interviewees with psychosocial disabilities were held in solitary — an NGO measuring SA prison practice against the Mandela Rules before Australia's next UN torture review.
core_labels: A contemporary issue illustrating the promotion and/or enforcement of human rights
items.document: Human Rights/HR - HRW Solitary Confinement Prisoners with Disabilities SA Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
HRW interviewed **42** people (June 2025 – June 2026) across nine SA prisons: **12 of 14** interviewees with psychosocial
disabilities had been held in solitary, **4** for 15 days or longer; a wheelchair user spent **8 days** without an
accessible bathroom. SA publishes no data on prisoners with disabilities; the Department refused HRW access to two
prisons and its reply is annexed.

items.title: NT and Queensland shut a UN expert out of youth detention (Amnesty International, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of an Amnesty International Australia media release, 2 November 2026, on the refusal of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples' requests to visit Holtze (NT) and Cleveland (Qld) youth detention centres; UNDRIP; OPCAT (ratified December 2017); CROC arts 37(b), 40(1)
items.significance: A UN expert invited to Australia was refused entry to two youth detention centres holding mostly First Nations children — the third UN access dispute since 2022.
core_labels: The role of the United Nations
items.document: Human Rights/HR - UN Rapporteur Refused Youth Detention Access Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The Special Rapporteur's official visit runs **2–13 November 2026**. The NT and Queensland refused planned visits to
**Holtze** and **Cleveland**, where about **97%** of children at Cleveland were Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander at
inspection. It is the second time in under a year the NT has blocked UN experts. First Nations young people are detained at **25.7 per 10,000** (2024–25), against a
Closing the Gap target of a 30% fall by 2031; the Productivity Commission assesses no change.
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.2 / hr.2.1** — UN monitoring inside a sovereign, federal state; the Commonwealth answers internationally for
  detention run by states and territories.
- **Year 11 (the global legal system)** — state sovereignty and the UN's role.
items.caution: A **class evidence summary of an NGO advocacy release**; no government explanation is included.

sections.What the mandate asks v what happened:
| UN terms of reference | November 2026 |
|---|---|
| Access to all places of detention | Holtze and Cleveland visits refused |
| Confidential contact with detainees | No in-centre contact with children |
| Contact with authorities in every branch | NT and Qld refused to engage, the Rapporteur says |
| Freedom of movement | Visit otherwise proceeding |
| Findings reported to the Human Rights Council | Precedent: the WGAD relied on public reports for the NT |

The terms of reference are UN guidelines, not a treaty: visits depend on the state's invitation and cooperation.

items.title: Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project take the under-16s social media ban to the High Court (The Guardian, 3 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Josh Taylor, The Guardian Australia, 3 November 2026, on Reddit, Inc v Commonwealth (S166/2025) and Digital Freedom Project Incorporated v Commonwealth (S163/2025), heard 3 and 4 November 2026; read with Part 4A of the Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) and eSafety's March 2026 survey
items.significance: Reddit and a libertarian group ask the High Court to strike down the under-16s social media ban, testing whether an implied freedom, not a bill of rights, can check a law protecting children.
core_labels: A contemporary issue illustrating the promotion and/or enforcement of human rights
items.document: Human Rights/HR - Reddit v under-16s ban (High Court) - hearing Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead: The first major legal challenge to the under-16s social media ban was heard in the High Court on **3 and 4 November 2026**. Australia has no guaranteed right to free speech, so both challengers rely on the **implied freedom of political communication**: they say stopping under-16s holding accounts burdens political communication, and the Commonwealth says the law serves a legitimate purpose, reducing harm from features such as algorithms, infinite scroll and notifications. **No decision has been made.**
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.8 The role of the Constitution**: no bill of rights, an implied freedom made by judges, and a court asked to weigh a new community value (child safety online) against it. Fits HSC 2024 Q22 (the Constitution and changing values); the summary's exemplar paragraph answers it.
- **hr.3.1 A contemporary issue**, with hr.2.11 (courts) and hr.2.9 (statute law); also compliance, as eSafety investigates five platforms.
items.caution: A preview of an **undecided case**, not a judgment: update this record when the Court rules. The parties' submissions could not be opened, so their arguments are as reported. Read from a saved copy of the Guardian article. The tests come from secondary summaries; check the High Court's reasons before quoting them.

sections.The two challenges:
| | Reddit | Digital Freedom Project (led by NSW Libertarian MP John Ruddick) |
|---|---|---|
| Argument | Platforms are a common source of political information; teens could not post, comment or react on politics | Adopts much the same argument on the burden on political communication |
| Hurdle | Whether the burden is justified | The Commonwealth says the group has **no standing**: it has not identified any activity of its own that is impeded. Its two teenage plaintiffs withdrew in July |
sections.How the court decides: An implied-freedom case asks, in turn: is there a burden on political communication; is the law's purpose legitimate; is it suitable, necessary and adequate in balance (the structured proportionality test from *McCloy v NSW* (2015)). Commentators are divided: Prof Anne Twomey saw a possible mismatch between purpose and effect; Prof Luke Beck expected the challenges to fail.
sections.The numbers, checked:
- **Ten** platforms had to restrict under-16 accounts from **10 December 2025**. The Prime Minister says more than **5 million** accounts were suspended; eSafety reported about **4.7 million** by mid-December 2025. These count accounts, not children.
- eSafety's March 2026 survey found the share of under-16s holding an account fell from **52.4% to 42.1%**: a modest but real fall, and evidence for both sides on whether the ban works.
- The maximum penalty was doubled from **$49.5 million to $99 million** by an Act assented to on 11 September 2026; the Guardian's "nearly $100m" is consistent.
- The government says the **digital duty of care** bill would "require the same action"; the bill is s…

| Purpose | Accept protecting young people is legitimate | Protects children from engagement-driven features |
| Effectiveness | Under-16s evade age checks; content still viewable logged out | Rules are consultative, targeted, adjustable |

items.title: Mother told to pay child support to an ex she says owes her $15,000 (ABC, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Tahlia Roy, ABC News, 2 November 2026; Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989 (Cth) ss 63A–64AH, 98B, 98C, 117(2); Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) s 4AB(2A); 2026–27 Budget child support package
items.significance: A low income estimate can reverse who pays: a mother says her abusive ex used the scheme's rules so she, the main carer, now owes him — a protective law turned into a tool of financial abuse.
items.document: Family/Evidence Summaries/Family - Child Support Financial Abuse (updated 4Nov26) Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
"Chloe" (a pseudonym) says her former partner's income fell on paper from more than **$300,000** to under
**$20,000** through income estimates, so that from November 2026 she — the main carer — must pay him. Financial
abuse is family violence under the *Family Law Act* (s 4AB(2A)).
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.2** — child support as a consequence of separation, and enforcement gaps.
- **fam.2.4** — systems abuse: legal processes used to continue control after separation.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of one parent's account**, not independently verified; neither the ex-partner nor
Services Australia responded on the case.

sections.Meant to work v can be misused:
| | How it should work | How it can be misused |
|---|---|---|
| Income estimates | Allowed only if income has fallen **15%+** | About **half** of 70,000 estimates a year are incorrect |
| Reconciliation | Replaced by actual income; 10% penalty if 110%+ | Needs tax returns — 200,000+ payers had not lodged for two years |
| Collection | Agency Collect enforces | Private Collect assumed paid; 70% of financially abused women on it not paid in full |
| Challenging income | Change of assessment (s 98C) | Burden falls on the victim-survivor to prove the other parent's income |

**$2.0 billion** in Agency Collect debt is owed by 229,235 paying parents (March 2026). The **$182.6m** 2026–27 reform
pa…
sections.Expert comment (4 November summary):
Dr **Amira Aftab** (Macquarie Law School) and **Amy Kilpatrick** (Care Financial and Consumer Law Centre) say the scheme's
trust in self-reported income and slow correction through tax returns leaves victim-survivors carrying the burden of
proof (change of assessment, s 117(2)). Agency Collect can garnish wages (Registration and Collection Act s 72D);
Private Collect is unmonitored, so the true debt is unknown. Chloe's bank statements were allegedly used to harass her
in the **property settlement**, not the child support assessment.

items.title: A rate hike to 4.85% tests legal protections for owners and renters (ABC live blog, 3 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of ABC News live coverage, 3 November 2026, with the RBA Monetary Policy Board decision; National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (Cth) ss 47, 131 and National Credit Code s 72; Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) ss 41, 43
items.significance: A fifth rate rise in 2026 adds about $456 a month to a $600,000 loan: borrowers have enforceable hardship rights and AFCA, but NSW renters face limits only on the timing, not the size, of increases.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - RBA Rate Hike and Housing Affordability Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
On **3 November 2026** the RBA lifted the cash rate 0.25 points to **4.85%** by a 6–3 vote — about **$456 a month**
more on a $600,000 loan than in January (Canstar). AFCA home loan complaints rose **21%** to 7,014 in 2025–26; Westpac
was penalised **$26m** for ignoring hardship notices.
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.1.4** — affordability and the cost of credit; **shel.2.1** — legal protections for borrowers.
- **Comparison** — owners' rights slow loss of the home; neither regime limits what shelter costs over time.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of rolling market coverage** that says little about legal rights; the legal framework comes
from the summary's other sources. Canstar figures were not checked against its release.

sections.Owners v renters:
| | Owner-occupier with a mortgage | NSW renter |
|---|---|---|
| How costs rise | Variable repayments rise as lenders pass hikes on | Only through the s 41 rent increase process |
| Limits | Serviceability buffer at approval; s 131 unsuitability test | Once per 12 months, 60 days' notice — **no cap on amount** |
| Hardship | **s 72 hardship notice**; written answer within 21 days | No hardship variation right; s 43 reduction only in limited cases |
| Disputes | **AFCA** (free); lender generally pauses enforcement | NCAT, judged against market rent |
| Losing the home | Default notice, 30 days to remedy | Reasonable ground needed since May 2025 |

items.title: NSW firearms reforms after Bondi and the National Gun Buyback (2025–2027)
items.citation: Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2025 (NSW) (passed 24 December 2025); National Gun Buyback, NSW Government media release, 26 October 2026, and joint Commonwealth–NSW release, 16 August 2026
items.significance: After the 14 December 2025 Bondi Beach terror attack, NSW capped gun numbers, cut licences to two years and removed NCAT review, then opened a buyback for up to 274,000 firearms.
core_labels: Overview of the area of law reform
Executive methods — political will, parliamentary debate, ministerial directions
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - National gun buyback after Bondi - day one (4Nov26) Evidence Summary.pdf
items.document11: Preliminary/Year 11 - National Gun Buyback Law Reform After Bondi Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The **Bondi Beach terrorist attack** on 14 December 2025 killed 15 people. Ten days later NSW passed the
**Terrorism and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2025**, and in August 2026 NSW became the first state to
join a **National Gun Buyback**, citing recommendations 13 and 14 of a Royal Commission interim report.
Bookings opened on 26 October 2026; surrenders run from **2 November 2026** at six police stations,
widening in stages to February 2027, for about 12 months.
items.use_it_for:
- **chg.6 (an area of law reform)** — event as a reason; Royal Commission recommendations and public
  opinion as drivers; **legislative** (the 2025 Act) and **executive** (the scheme) methods.
- **chg.4.1 / chg.4.2** — fewer guns against fixed compensation (one farmer paid $2,900 for a gun worth
  $850 under the schedule), uneven national uptake (Queensland, Victoria and the NT declined) and
  divided research on the 1996 Port Arthur buyback.
- **inv.5.2** — a state law with a Commonwealth-funded scheme: division of powers and cooperation.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a government media release** with a political purpose; it omits prices
and partisan claims are disputed. The 18% of licence holders and $42.8 million Registry figures are
unverified. Several provisions await proclamation and the cap-exception regulation is unfinished.

sections.Before and after:
| | Before | After the 2025 Act |
|---|---|---|
| Number of guns | No fixed cap | **4** (recreational hunting, vermin) or **10** (most other genuine reasons); collectors and dealers unlimited |
| Licence term | Up to 5 years | **2 years** (licences from 1 July 2026) |
| Review of decisions | External appeal to **NCAT** | Internal review only (except Firearm Prohibition Orders) |
| Permit to acquire | — | Safe-storage inspection and terrorism-related checks first |
| Categories | Straight-pull, pump, lever-release lower | Moved to Category C; belt-fed prohibited |
| Club membership | Not required for all A/B holders | Required once proclaimed |
sections.Day one (2 November 2026):
The buyback began on **2 November 2026** at six stations (Dubbo, Griffith, Grafton, Penrith, Sutherland, Narellan),
with 34 more from early December; initial bookings were **full on day one**. The Act (No 86 of 2025) was rushed
through in **three days** after Bondi. The Premier expects the demand-driven scheme to cost "hundreds of millions";
existing owners above the caps face no immediate seizure, and permits to exceed them await regulations. The caps have

Notice letter → book through the **Gun Safe** portal (no walk-ins) → surrender at a station → fixed

guns) could be surrendered.

## Day one (2 November 2026)

The buyback began on **2 November 2026** at six stations (Dubbo, Griffith, Grafton, Penrith, Sutherland, Narellan),
with 34 more from early December; initial bookings were **full on day one**. The Act (No 86 of 2025) was rushed
through in **three days** after Bondi. The Premier expects the demand-driven scheme to cost "hundreds of millions";
existing owners above the caps face no immediate seizure, and permits to exceed them await regulations. The caps have
become an **election issue** that the Opposition says it would revisit — a reform that may be reversed.

Firearms theft is part of the crime-prevention case: **417** firearms were stolen in NSW in 2024 (about **1.1 a day**).
Removing NCAT review narrows external checks on police licensing decisions. Phase two (from 2027) pays up to
$10,000 for higher-value firearms.
